newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian inflation falls but not yet tamed.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian inflation falls but not yet tamed.

text.p: Inflation, long the torment of Nigerias economy, has fallen steadily over the last year but analysts warn that it is too early to consider it contained.

Finance minister Anthony Ani reported this week that annual inflation fell to 26 percent in January from 29 percent in December. He said the rate was falling by 3.5 percentage points a month and was expected to drop to between 12 and 15 percent by mid-year.
"There is no doubt that inflation has been heading downwards which is good news but the ministers projection is a very optimistic one," said banker Kukoyi Edu.
"The main worry is the level of liquidity which is very high currently and may soon begin to push inflation up again," said Justine Igere, who operates several retail shops in Lagos.
Taming inflation has been the cardinal policy of the military government since 1995 when recession and political crisis combined to push annual inflation to well above 70 percent.
The indicator began to fall last year when the government squeezed public spending while aggressively mopping up money in circulation through weekly sales of treasury bills.
Other fiscal measures such as a weekly foreign exchange auction have helped to bring stability to several facets of the economy including the exchange rate of the naira.
Interest rates were freed and are currently well below the 21 percent at which they were pegged by fiat until late 1996.

By Christmas consumer prices of many key commodities were noticeably lower. A 50 kg bag of rice was selling at 2,500 naira ($31), down from 3,500 naira at the beginning of the year, but that price was still above the purchasing power of many people because of the cash squeeze.
Economists argue that the growth of 3.25 percent in gross domestic production in 1996 was not enough to improve the living conditions of ordinary Nigerians.
So the government, aiming for growth of 5.5 percent in 1997, last month announced a reflationary budget, including spending some of the 37 billion naira budget surplus accumulated in 1996.
Nevertheless, the government remains determined to fight inflation to ensure goods and services are affordable by most of Nigerians.

"You are right that we should be careful not to reflate the economy in such a way as to stimulate inflation," said central bank governor Paul Ogwuma in a recent interview with the independent Thisday newspaper.
"But youll find out that there is no amount of reflation that will result in major inflationary trend in 1997. We expect that inflation will be as near in check as possible," he added.
Development economist Benjamin Umoh said if carefully implemented the Nigerian package may not necessarily stoke inflation.
"Despite the money they are putting into the economy, the monetary policy is actually quite lean and mean because they have a tight control on what it will be spent on," he said.
His view is shared by Ibrahim Ida, secretary of the Vision 2010 committee which is charged with planning Nigerias economic future.
"The government is checking the inflow of money into the economy to continue to curb the inflationary rate," he told Reuters in the capital Abuja.
"This is why the release of funds is only for budgeted projects and the payment of debts. So no surplus money is in circulation," he said.

The new budget shifts government spending dramatically to rural areas and to the repair of public infrastructure, which the government hopes will have a positive impact on living conditions in the villages.
Billions of naira have also been voted to pay long-owed debts to local contractors and official debts to banks.
Under a new policy to stem a tide of failures the banks have have been ordered to increase their capital base by 900 percent or risk liquidation by December 1998.
"The recapitalisation of the banks means they have to watch every kobo (cent) they have," said Umoh.

Bankers said the key unknown quantity for the economy remained the political crisis unleashed after June 1993 when a previous army government annulled a presidential poll aimed at restoring democracy.

Military ruler General Sani Abacha last year pledged to hand over to a democratically-elected president and registration of voters for future polls has commenced. But uncertainty about the transition persists with the continued detention of Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled vote.
Bomb blasts linked to the crisis have rocked Lagos in the last three months killing three soldiers and wounding many.
"The political crisis is the unknown quantity and how it plays out will be crucial to the economy and inflation," said Edu. ($=79.9 naira) --Lagos newsroom +234 1 2630317
